new.title: Find Grutte Pier's sword in the Fries Museum
new.desc: Friesland's big regional museum holds over a million objects, from the glittering Popta silver treasure to the enormous sword of the rebel giant Pier Gerlofs Donia.
new.tip: Look for the Mata Hari room before you leave; her birthplace is a short walk away.

new.title: Hear the Müller organ in the Jacobijnerkerk
new.desc: Leeuwarden's great medieval church dates back to around 1300 and is the oldest building in the city. Inside, the stained glass and the 1727 organ by Christian Müller are the stars.
new.tip: Entry is free when the church is open; check for summer organ concerts.

new.title: Meet Mata Hari on the Kelders
new.desc: The famous dancer and alleged spy was born in Leeuwarden, where her father ran a hat shop at Kelders 33. A bronze statue of her mid dance stands by the canal in front of the house.
new.tip: It's free to see the statue; pair it with the Mata Hari room in the Fries Museum.
new.q: Mata Hari statue Over de Kelders Leeuwarden

new.title: Walk through the mist of Plensa's Love fountain
new.desc: Right outside the station, two seven-metre white figures of a boy and a girl with closed eyes rise from a veil of mist. Jaume Plensa made them for 11Fountains, a set of artworks in all eleven Elfsteden cities.
new.tip: Use it as the first stop of a fountain hunt: Sneek, Franeker, Harlingen and Dokkum have their own 11Fountains pieces.

new.title: Look up at the 85-metre spire of the Bonifatiuskerk
new.desc: Pierre Cuypers, architect of the Rijksmuseum, built this neo-Gothic basilica in the 1880s. A storm blew its wooden spire down in 1976, and it was rebuilt exactly as it was.
new.tip: Step inside if the doors are open; the choir organ is a rare Cavaillé-Coll instrument.

new.title: Dunk a Fryske dúmke at De Grutterswinkel
new.desc: This grocery shop of the Feenstra sisters closed in 1973 and was kept just as it was, marble counters, old tins and all. Today it is a museum where you can still buy nostalgic products and have coffee with a dúmke, the Frisian aniseed biscuit.
new.tip: Ask about the pram in the upstairs bedroom; it hides a wartime secret.

new.title: Lunch in the old weigh house on the Nieuwestad
new.desc: The Waag of 1598 once weighed the butter and cheese that made Leeuwarden rich. It now serves lunch in the heart of the city, right on the canal.
new.tip: On sunny days grab a terrace seat and watch the boats on the Nieuwestad canal.

new.title: Raise a glass at In De Brouwerij
new.desc: Leeuwarden once had more than a hundred breweries, and this beer café on the Zaailand keeps that memory alive with a long list of beers. It also has a small boutique hotel in the old coach house.
new.tip: Ask for a Frisian beer, or end the evening with a Beerenburg.

new.title: Dive under the Frisian waters at the Natuurmuseum
new.desc: Four floors of Frisian nature lead to the OnderWaterSafari, a dark ride that takes you under the water of ditches, lakes and the Wadden Sea. A sperm whale skeleton from an Ameland beach hangs in its own hall.
new.tip: Climb to the attic to find Li-Ming, a 14-metre dragon; children love it.

new.title: Hunt for the Miniature People of Leeuwarden
new.desc: Photographer Michel Tilma has hidden more than fifty tiny figure scenes in corners, gutters and windowsills all over the centre. Spotting them turns a city walk into a treasure hunt.
new.tip: Pick up the paper route map in town, or follow the virtual route on Google Maps.

new.title: Stroll the Prinsentuin to the Pier Pander temple
new.desc: The Prinsentuin was once the private garden of the Frisian stadtholders. Follow the moat to the Noorderplantage, where a small temple holds five marble figures by the Frisian sculptor Pier Pander.
new.tip: Summer Sunday afternoons often bring free concerts in the Prinsentuin; De Koperen Tuin is the park café.

new.title: Skipper an electric sloop through the Leeuwarden canals
new.desc: Leeuwarden is ringed by its old moat and crossed by canals, and the best view of its gables is from the water. You can rent a quiet electric sloop yourself, no licence needed.
new.tip: Book through the tourist information office, which also suggests routes; prefer a guided ride? The Praamverhuur canal tour shows old photos on a screen as you pass.

new.title: See the steam giant of Lemmer, the Woudagemaal
new.desc: Opened by Queen Wilhelmina in 1920, this is the largest steam pumping station ever built and still keeps Friesland dry when the water gets too high. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
new.tip: The visitor centre is open regularly, but the real show is a day when the engines are under steam; those dates are announced ahead.

new.title: Walk the ramparts of tiny Sloten
new.desc: Friesland's smallest city has kept almost all of its ramparts and moat, laid out by Menno van Coehoorn in an onion shape. The De Kaai windmill guards the water gate by a monumental bridge.
new.tip: The whole town is a twenty-minute walk; come on the last Saturday of June for the Sipelsneon fair.

new.title: Greet the proud Vrouwtje van Stavoren
new.desc: Legend says a rich widow of Stavoren had a cargo of grain dumped in the sea and threw her ring after it, only to find it in a fish and lose everything. Her statue from 1969 still stares out over the water.
new.tip: In summer the ferry to Enkhuizen sails from Stavoren, so you can arrive by boat across the IJsselmeer.

new.title: Meet Jopie Huisman's worn-out treasures in Workum
new.desc: The self-taught painter and rag-and-bone man from Workum painted old shoes, clothes and dolls with loving precision. His museum was one of the first in the country dedicated to a living artist.
new.tip: Don't miss the rebuilt barn with the real objects from his paintings; afterwards walk to the harbour of Workum.

new.title: Look up at the Brandaris on Terschelling
new.desc: Finished in 1594, the Brandaris still towers over the rooftops of West-Terschelling and guides ships today. It was the first in the country to get a rotating Fresnel lens.
new.tip: It's a few minutes' walk from the ferry; at night watch its beam sweep across the harbour.

new.title: Visit the mummies of Wieuwerd
new.desc: Under the medieval church of the tiny village of Wieuwerd (Wiuwert) lie four bodies that mummified naturally in the 17th century, nobody quite knows how. Even birds hung in the crypt as a test turned into mummies.
new.tip: Opening times are limited, so check mummiekelder.nl before you cycle out from Leeuwarden.

new.title: Taste Us Heit beer and Frisian whisky in Bolsward
new.desc: This family brewery has made Frisian specialty beers since 1985, and also distils Frysk Hynder, Friesland's single malt whisky. Everything comes as far as possible from local farmers.
new.tip: Tours run by reservation only; drop by the tasting room and shop on the Snekerstraat otherwise.

new.title: Crunch a drabbelkoek from Haga in Sneek
new.desc: Drabbelkoeken are hard, buttery cinnamon biscuits made by dribbling batter into hot butter, and they belong to Sneek. The Haga factory has baked them since 1850, the oldest maker of the recipe.
new.tip: Buy a tin to take home; the factory is on the 1e Oosterkade, close to the Waterpoort.

new.title: Buy fresh-roasted coffee where Douwe Egberts began
new.desc: The coffee brand Douwe Egberts was born in Joure. Museum Joure tells the story in old warehouses, and De Witte Os, the former company shop, still sells freshly roasted coffee, loose tea and old-fashioned sweets.
new.tip: Egbert Douwes's birth house was moved into the museum garden; the café is in the same building as the ticket desk.
new.q: Museum Joure De Witte Os Midstraat Joure

new.title: Drink island beer brewed with Terschelling dune water
new.desc: Behind restaurant Storm in West-Terschelling, the small Schoemrakker brewery makes its beer the traditional way with water from the island's dunes. You'll find it in cafés all over the island.
new.tip: Order one with a meal at Storm on the Torenstraat, right next to the Brandaris.

new.title: Eat island flavours at Ambrosijn on Schiermonnikoog
new.desc: In the car-free village, Ambrosijn is a restaurant, ice cream parlour and small hotel in one, cooking with seasonal produce and seafood from around the island.
new.tip: Come for lunch and the shellfish broth, or just grab an ice cream on your bike ride through the village.

new.title: Walk across the Wadden Sea seabed from Holwerd
new.desc: At low tide you can hike over the mudflats of the Wadden Sea, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, wading through channels toward Ameland or the sandbank of the Engelsmanplaat. With luck you see seals along the way.
new.tip: Only go with a licensed guide; Holwerd and Paesens-Moddergat are the usual starting points, and old trainers and shorts are the right outfit.

new.title: Watch the fierljeppers fly over the ditch in IJlst
new.desc: Fierljeppen is Friesland's own sport: sprint, grab a tall pole planted in a canal, climb it and land as far as possible on the other bank, or in the water. The best jumpers clear more than twenty metres.
new.tip: Competitions run at the schans on the Sudergoweg in summer; bring a folding chair, and note that there is no jumping in the rain.

new.title: Ride the Elfstedentocht route by bike from Bolsward
new.desc: The legendary skating race hardly ever happens, but every Whit Monday up to 15,000 cyclists ride the 235 km Fietselfstedentocht past all eleven Frisian cities, collecting stamps on the way.
new.tip: Registration has a lottery, so sign up early; otherwise ride the signposted route at your own pace over a few days.

new.title: Cheer on the skaters at Thialf in Heerenveen
new.desc: Skating is Friesland's favourite sport, and Thialf is its temple: a covered 400-metre oval where world records fall and orange-clad crowds roar. It hosts the speed skating events of the 2030 Winter Olympics.
new.tip: Catch a World Cup or national championship weekend; the atmosphere in the stands is unforgettable.

new.title: See horses launch the lifeboat on Ameland
new.desc: Since 1824 Hollum's lifeboat was dragged into the surf by horses. A team of ten horses still pulls the boat 'Abraham Fock' through the waves in demonstrations that the whole island turns out for.
new.tip: Watching is free; the parade leaves from the Maritiem Centrum Abraham Fock on the Oranjeweg, and the launch is at the end of the Tjettepad. Check the dates first.
